records.content: The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. Mississippi State brings aquatic health experts together to combat antibiotic resistance in aquaculture and advance veterinary disease prevention. Researchers at the University of South Florida are developing an experimental gene therapy designed to protect aging brain cells and potentially slow canine cognitive decline. If successful, the approach could offer veterinarians something they've long needed: a way to target the disease itself rather than simply manage its symptoms. After serving in the U.S. Navy, raising a family while earning her veterinary degree, and drawing inspiration from her immigrant mother's entrepreneurial journey, Dr. Lieu Balu is preparing to lead her own veterinary clinic in Phoenix. Scientists detect H5 bird flu antibodies in apparently healthy Greenland polar bears, raising new concerns about wildlife disease spread in the Arctic. In the 1970s, researchers began to observe drastic amphibian declines in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, a global hotspot of frog biodiversity. For decades, these disappearances remained a mystery. Ask most people what a veterinary pathologist does all day and they’ll probably picture microscopes, slides, cells, and very serious diagnostic reports. Dr. Aleksandra Zuraw certainly does all of that. The FDA has approved a new, more concentrated, ready-to-use version of Convenia that delivers up to 14 days of antibiotic treatment in a single injection. The new formulation could make managing bacterial skin infections easier for veterinarians and dog owners, especially when larger dogs need treatment. New research reveals that veterinary students aren't necessarily losing their passion for horses. They're questioning whether equine medicine can offer the salary, mentorship, respect, and work-life balance they need to build a sustainable career. The veterinary profession has already seen what can happen when this virus crosses the animal-human barrier. During the devastating 1998–1999 outbreak in Malaysia, infected pigs played a central role in transmitting Nipah virus to humans. The outbreak led to the culling of more than one million pigs and caused estimated economic losses of £433 million, approximately $582 million. 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. Vet school can turn almost anything into a performance metric. Grades, class rank, clinical skills, productivity, sleep, exercise, and sometimes even food can quietly become one more thing you feel like you should be “doing right.” Add long days, irregular schedules, stress, limited money, constant comparison, and a culture that can reward pushing through discomfort, and it is easy for a complicated relationship with food or your body to hide in plain sight. There are queer and trans veterinarians who came before you, students at other schools experiencing many of the same things, peer-support volunteers willing to listen, community organizations that know your city, and national groups that can help when a problem becomes medical, legal, academic, or overwhelming. Vet school has a way of eating your entire calendar. Between exams, labs, rotations, boards, jobs, relationships, and trying to get enough sleep to remain functional, personal health can slide down the priority list pretty quickly. There is a particular kind of kitchen alchemy that happens when nothing gets thrown away: a roast chicken becomes dinner, then lunch, then the broth for Thursday's ramen. A single Sunday afternoon becomes a month of breakfasts. What follows is not a diet plan so much as a system, one built on a $500 monthly grocery budget, a single person's appetite, and the stubborn belief that homemade is both cheaper and better. Meet Mecca Gladney, a first-generation college graduate, mother, and University of Arizona veterinary student pursuing a career in veterinary surgery while championing representation, mentorship, and mental health. The UC Davis veterinary student took a winding road to her dream school, but every setback helped shape the veterinarian and mentor she hopes to become. Now Monika Lagarejos wants to use her place in veterinary medicine to care for animals, strengthen communities, and make sure the next generation of future veterinarians knows they belong. McPaul Hermoso started veterinary school at 35 after earning multiple degrees and living in five countries. Discover his unconventional journey, lifelong dream of becoming a veterinarian, and mission to inspire others. From four years cheering at LSU to studying veterinary medicine at the Royal Veterinary College, Jalyne Blackwell is building a career by saying yes to the opportunities that scare her a little—and trusting that the unexpected path might be the right one. After France’s competitive exams shut the door, this 20-year-old found her calling 800 miles from home — and proof that a detour can still lead exactly where you were meant to go. Meet Taja Bell, an LSU veterinary student, Army Animal Care Specialist, mom and model working toward a future in emergency medicine and surgery. There is a particular kind of courage it takes to walk away from a career you have already proven yourself in and start over as a first-year student. Emese Avdeyenkova has done exactly that, twice over, once when she traded a biology degree for an Army uniform, and again when she traded that uniform for a white coat. Now she is bringing all of it, the discipline, the humility, and the hard-won perspective, to Vet Candy Radio as one of the vet student hosts of Vet School After Dark. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Every NAVLE Warrior asks some version of the same question during week six: am I studying the right way, or am I just studying the most? Cognitive science has a real answer to that question, and it is not the one most students expect Every NAVLE study plan is built around content: which species, which systems, which diagnoses to drill. But the brain that has to hold all of that information is a physical organ, and it runs on three inputs: sleep, movement, and nutrition. Neglect any one of them and the same number of practice questions will produce worse results. Here's the science behind why, and what to actually do about it. Starting with the October to November 2026 testing window, the NAVLE looks different in two ways that actually matter for how you study. The exam moved to a new block format back in the spring update, and now the ICVA has also refreshed the Species and Diagnosis list itself, adding more than 100 diseases across the species you'll be tested on. That is not a small revision. That is the blueprint growing, and it means the way you have been prepping needs a second look. Paid NAVLE prep services can cost more than $600 for a thirty month pass, sometimes more. For companies selling them, that is a subscription. For a fourth-year veterinary student, that can be groceries for two months. And in a year when gas prices and food prices have squeezed every budget in America, plenty of vet students are doing math far scarier than anything on the exam. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. This particular offering from Vet Candy lands firmly in the second category. Based on a short story by Vet Candy’s CEO and X-Files super fan, Dr. Jill Lopez. Dr. Joya Griffin and Dr. Forrest Cummings just dropped the veterinary CE series that changes how you think about complex cases and it is free with your Vet Candy membership. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Unleash Your Inner Hero! , an 8-module urgent care program led by veterinary criticalist Dr. Natosha Richardson. Offering 3.5 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians, this course covers triage, CPR, supportive care, diagnostics, and treatment across neurologic, gastrointestinal, respiratory, and integumentary emergencies. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Dermatology Secrets featuring Dr. Joya Griffin. This three-part online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers the dermatology skills that matter most in everyday practice — skin cytology, histopathology and biopsy interpretation, and the strangest and most diagnostically challenging cases in specialist dermatology. Learn how to read a cytology slide with confidence, decode a dermatopathology report, and work through complex skin presentations that have not responded to standard treatment. Earn 1.5 RACE CE credits at no cost with your free Vet Candy Membership! Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with the Respiratory Disease Master Course featuring Criticalist Dr. Anthony Gonzalez. Brought to you by Trudell Animal Health, this 8-module course provides 4 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians. It covers recognition, diagnosis, and management of acute and chronic respiratory disease, including practical guidance on critical care, advanced monitoring, oxygen therapy, and evidence-based treatment strategies. Designed for immediate clinical application, this course helps veterinary professionals improve outcomes in high-stakes respiratory cases. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Endocrinology Secrets featuring Dr. Forrest Cummings. This online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers real-world management of diabetes in dogs and cats, Cushing’s disease, and Addison’s disease. Learn how to interpret diagnostics, manage challenging endocrine cases, and improve patient outcomes with practical, case-based guidance. Earn 2 RACE CE credits at no cost—no subscription or credit card required. The Gut-Brain connection is more connected than we thought. This episode of Catching Up explores the fascinating link between the gut and brain in pets. Could your patient's GI issues be tied to behavior? The science says yes. Acute Kidney Injury Alert: New Biomarkers That Could Save Lives. Dr. Elan Armstrong & Dr. Shannon Gregoire break down the newest research on acute kidney injury. World-First Breakthrough: Stem Cells from Cats Could Revolutionize Kidney Disease Treatment! Vet Candy has the details with Dr. Elan & Dr. Shannon. Big news in hemangiosarcoma research! Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. Presented by Zoetis, maker of Solensia. SolensiaVetTeam.com A cat eye that won't heal is one of those cases that can quietly spiral into something serious — fast. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Veterinary emergency specialist Dr. Kristin Welch walks through a real hyperglycemia case that didn't follow the textbook. Watch the diagnostic reasoning unfold on Vet Candy's Mystery Case Rounds. Dr. Ashley Bourgeois breaks down what is really going on when a Pomeranian loses its coat, the hormonal, genetic, and inflammatory factors may be at play, why this breed is uniquely predisposed to certain dermatologic conditions, and how to build a workup that actually leads somewhere instead of chasing your tail. Nearly a quarter of homeless youth in the U.S. have pets — and some choose veterinary care over their own health care. The Seattle One Health Clinic offers both, side by side, for free. Jeremiah Pouncy shares why this One Health model is changing how we think about the human-animal bond and community care. In Barcelona, scientists are building a biological deep freeze for endangered species, storing genetic material from nearly 300 species and using AI to unlock the future of conservation. Jeremiah Pouncy explains how the Barcelona CryoZoo could change everything we know about saving wildlife from extinction. With fewer than 800 left on Earth, the Bengal florican is one of the rarest birds alive. But in India's Manas National Park, over 800 former poachers have become the species' fiercest protectors. Jeremiah Pouncy tells the remarkable story of how community-led conservation turned a near-extinction into a comeback. A new study on the "Capitoline dolphins" off Rome's coast reveals a population in crisis. Seven out of ten show signs of malnutrition, many bear scars from fishing gear, and scientists warn they may disappear without urgent intervention. Jeremiah Pouncy breaks down what is threatening one of the world's most historically significant dolphin populations and why it matters. Going back to veterinary school usually means new classes, new rotations, new schedules, and the familiar feeling that summer disappeared way too fast. For the hosts of Vet School After Dark , it also means catching up on where everyone spent the break and figuring out how to mentally transition back into another demanding academic year. Vet Candy's hit podcast recently went live in Nashville, and what started as another fast-paced battle of veterinary knowledge quickly turned into something no one in the room saw coming. Dr. Lauren Downey Koos didn't have to look far to get to WVC Nashville. She works at BluePearl Veterinary in Franklin, Tennessee, which means the conference is essentially in her backyard. She graduated from the University of Florida in 2018, went into neurology, and became a specialist faster than most people finish paying off their student loans. Hosts Caitlin and Clay Palme…

records.content: The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. Mississippi State brings aquatic health experts together to combat antibiotic resistance in aquaculture and advance veterinary disease prevention. Researchers at the University of South Florida are developing an experimental gene therapy designed to protect aging brain cells and potentially slow canine cognitive decline. If successful, the approach could offer veterinarians something they've long needed: a way to target the disease itself rather than simply manage its symptoms. After serving in the U.S. Navy, raising a family while earning her veterinary degree, and drawing inspiration from her immigrant mother's entrepreneurial journey, Dr. Lieu Balu is preparing to lead her own veterinary clinic in Phoenix. Scientists detect H5 bird flu antibodies in apparently healthy Greenland polar bears, raising new concerns about wildlife disease spread in the Arctic. In the 1970s, researchers began to observe drastic amphibian declines in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, a global hotspot of frog biodiversity. For decades, these disappearances remained a mystery. Ask most people what a veterinary pathologist does all day and they’ll probably picture microscopes, slides, cells, and very serious diagnostic reports. Dr. Aleksandra Zuraw certainly does all of that. The FDA has approved a new, more concentrated, ready-to-use version of Convenia that delivers up to 14 days of antibiotic treatment in a single injection. The new formulation could make managing bacterial skin infections easier for veterinarians and dog owners, especially when larger dogs need treatment. New research reveals that veterinary students aren't necessarily losing their passion for horses. They're questioning whether equine medicine can offer the salary, mentorship, respect, and work-life balance they need to build a sustainable career. The veterinary profession has already seen what can happen when this virus crosses the animal-human barrier. During the devastating 1998–1999 outbreak in Malaysia, infected pigs played a central role in transmitting Nipah virus to humans. The outbreak led to the culling of more than one million pigs and caused estimated economic losses of £433 million, approximately $582 million. 11 careers. 6 questions. Zero chill. Veterinary medicine isn't one job—it's about eleven careers hiding under the same white coat. There is a conversation happening in break rooms, group chats, and parking lots all over veterinary medicine. It usually starts the same way. I love the medicine, but I do not know how much longer I can do this. And it usually ends with a quiet assumption that something is wrong with the person saying it. Somewhere along the way, veterinary medicine developed an unwritten rule: clinical practice is the real job, and everything else is quitting. It gets absorbed in school, reinforced in practice, and carried around as guilt by veterinarians who are exhausted, curious, or simply ready for a change but afraid that stepping out of the exam room means abandoning their oath. If you are graduating this year, the offers are probably already arriving, and some of the numbers are eye-watering. Signing bonuses have become the headline of new grad recruitment, and with student debt where it is, nobody could blame you for reading the biggest number and reaching for a pen. Vet school can turn almost anything into a performance metric. Grades, class rank, clinical skills, productivity, sleep, exercise, and sometimes even food can quietly become one more thing you feel like you should be “doing right.” Add long days, irregular schedules, stress, limited money, constant comparison, and a culture that can reward pushing through discomfort, and it is easy for a complicated relationship with food or your body to hide in plain sight. There are queer and trans veterinarians who came before you, students at other schools experiencing many of the same things, peer-support volunteers willing to listen, community organizations that know your city, and national groups that can help when a problem becomes medical, legal, academic, or overwhelming. Vet school has a way of eating your entire calendar. Between exams, labs, rotations, boards, jobs, relationships, and trying to get enough sleep to remain functional, personal health can slide down the priority list pretty quickly. There is a particular kind of kitchen alchemy that happens when nothing gets thrown away: a roast chicken becomes dinner, then lunch, then the broth for Thursday's ramen. A single Sunday afternoon becomes a month of breakfasts. What follows is not a diet plan so much as a system, one built on a $500 monthly grocery budget, a single person's appetite, and the stubborn belief that homemade is both cheaper and better. Meet Mecca Gladney, a first-generation college graduate, mother, and University of Arizona veterinary student pursuing a career in veterinary surgery while championing representation, mentorship, and mental health. The UC Davis veterinary student took a winding road to her dream school, but every setback helped shape the veterinarian and mentor she hopes to become. Now Monika Lagarejos wants to use her place in veterinary medicine to care for animals, strengthen communities, and make sure the next generation of future veterinarians knows they belong. McPaul Hermoso started veterinary school at 35 after earning multiple degrees and living in five countries. Discover his unconventional journey, lifelong dream of becoming a veterinarian, and mission to inspire others. From four years cheering at LSU to studying veterinary medicine at the Royal Veterinary College, Jalyne Blackwell is building a career by saying yes to the opportunities that scare her a little—and trusting that the unexpected path might be the right one. After France’s competitive exams shut the door, this 20-year-old found her calling 800 miles from home — and proof that a detour can still lead exactly where you were meant to go. Meet Taja Bell, an LSU veterinary student, Army Animal Care Specialist, mom and model working toward a future in emergency medicine and surgery. There is a particular kind of courage it takes to walk away from a career you have already proven yourself in and start over as a first-year student. Emese Avdeyenkova has done exactly that, twice over, once when she traded a biology degree for an Army uniform, and again when she traded that uniform for a white coat. Now she is bringing all of it, the discipline, the humility, and the hard-won perspective, to Vet Candy Radio as one of the vet student hosts of Vet School After Dark. America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dig into the real science, history, and psychology behind humanity's longest-running obsession. We're talking ancient Egypt, where cats were literally worshipped as gods. We're talking the internet, where cats generate more content than almost anything else on the planet. From ancient worship to TikTok stardom, cats have clawed their way into our hearts and honestly, they never asked for permission. But why? What is it about the most indifferent creature on the planet that makes humans absolutely lose their minds? Think black cats bring bad luck? Think again. The truth about black cats is stranger, richer, and way more interesting than the superstition and Caitlin and Clay are here to set the record straight. In this episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer and her cat daddy husband Clay Palmer dive deep into the wild world of cat mythology, feline folklore, and the weirdest cat superstitions that humans have carried for centuries. We are talking black cats across cultures — feared in some, worshipped in others. We are talking mythological cats from ancient Egypt to Norse legends to the shadowy corners of the internet. We are talking the real history behind the myths that still follow these animals into shelters today, where black cats consistently wait the longest for homes. Spoiler: the cats were never the problem. Think you know everything about cats? In this hilarious episode of Cat Cafe, America's favorite vet receptionist Caitlin Palmer takes on the ultimate cat trivia challenge — and her cat daddy husband Clay is putting her knowledge to the test. From quirky cat facts to surprising feline science, this quiz will challenge even the most devoted cat lovers. Play along and see if you can beat America’s favorite veterinary receptionist, Caitlin Palmer! But it's not just fun and games. Every wrong answer comes with a punishment — and that punishment is pickle juice. Yes, really. Watch to find out who walks away victorious and who walks away regretting their cat knowledge gaps. • Fun (and tricky) cat trivia questions • Surprising cat facts you probably didn’t know • A very questionable pickle juice challenge Who’s the ultimate cat nerd... and who’s about to drink pickle juice? In this hilarious episode of Pet Candy, Caitlin and Clay go head-to-head in a cat trivia challenge with a twist—get a question wrong, and you have to take a sip of pickle juice Think you know cats? Play along and see if you can beat them (without the punishment.) Every NAVLE Warrior asks some version of the same question during week six: am I studying the right way, or am I just studying the most? Cognitive science has a real answer to that question, and it is not the one most students expect Every NAVLE study plan is built around content: which species, which systems, which diagnoses to drill. But the brain that has to hold all of that information is a physical organ, and it runs on three inputs: sleep, movement, and nutrition. Neglect any one of them and the same number of practice questions will produce worse results. Here's the science behind why, and what to actually do about it. Starting with the October to November 2026 testing window, the NAVLE looks different in two ways that actually matter for how you study. The exam moved to a new block format back in the spring update, and now the ICVA has also refreshed the Species and Diagnosis list itself, adding more than 100 diseases across the species you'll be tested on. That is not a small revision. That is the blueprint growing, and it means the way you have been prepping needs a second look. Paid NAVLE prep services can cost more than $600 for a thirty month pass, sometimes more. For companies selling them, that is a subscription. For a fourth-year veterinary student, that can be groceries for two months. And in a year when gas prices and food prices have squeezed every budget in America, plenty of vet students are doing math far scarier than anything on the exam. There are continuing education programs, and then there are continuing education programs where you accidentally debunk a mythical creature between bites of fried dough. This particular offering from Vet Candy lands firmly in the second category. Based on a short story by Vet Candy’s CEO and X-Files super fan, Dr. Jill Lopez. Dr. Joya Griffin and Dr. Forrest Cummings just dropped the veterinary CE series that changes how you think about complex cases and it is free with your Vet Candy membership. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Unleash Your Inner Hero! , an 8-module urgent care program led by veterinary criticalist Dr. Natosha Richardson. Offering 3.5 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians, this course covers triage, CPR, supportive care, diagnostics, and treatment across neurologic, gastrointestinal, respiratory, and integumentary emergencies. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Dermatology Secrets featuring Dr. Joya Griffin. This three-part online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers the dermatology skills that matter most in everyday practice — skin cytology, histopathology and biopsy interpretation, and the strangest and most diagnostically challenging cases in specialist dermatology. Learn how to read a cytology slide with confidence, decode a dermatopathology report, and work through complex skin presentations that have not responded to standard treatment. Earn 1.5 RACE CE credits at no cost with your free Vet Candy Membership! Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with the Respiratory Disease Master Course featuring Criticalist Dr. Anthony Gonzalez. Brought to you by Trudell Animal Health, this 8-module course provides 4 RACE CE credits for veterinarians and veterinary technicians. It covers recognition, diagnosis, and management of acute and chronic respiratory disease, including practical guidance on critical care, advanced monitoring, oxygen therapy, and evidence-based treatment strategies. Designed for immediate clinical application, this course helps veterinary professionals improve outcomes in high-stakes respiratory cases. Free RACE-approved veterinary CE is now available on Vet Candy with Endocrinology Secrets featuring Dr. Forrest Cummings. This online course is designed for veterinarians and veterinary technicians and covers real-world management of diabetes in dogs and cats, Cushing’s disease, and Addison’s disease. Learn how to interpret diagnostics, manage challenging endocrine cases, and improve patient outcomes with practical, case-based guidance. Earn 2 RACE CE credits at no cost—no subscription or credit card required. The Gut-Brain connection is more connected than we thought. This episode of Catching Up explores the fascinating link between the gut and brain in pets. Could your patient's GI issues be tied to behavior? The science says yes. Acute Kidney Injury Alert: New Biomarkers That Could Save Lives. Dr. Elan Armstrong & Dr. Shannon Gregoire break down the newest research on acute kidney injury. World-First Breakthrough: Stem Cells from Cats Could Revolutionize Kidney Disease Treatment! Vet Candy has the details with Dr. Elan & Dr. Shannon. Big news in hemangiosarcoma research! Tune in as we cover a promising breakthrough that could change the way we approach this aggressive cancer. Inside: Dr. Wailani Sung helps you learn how to Recognize the Subtle Signs of Pain in Cats. Presented by Zoetis, maker of Solensia. SolensiaVetTeam.com A cat eye that won't heal is one of those cases that can quietly spiral into something serious — fast. In this episode of Rounds with Dr. Shannon, Dr. Shannon Gregoire sits down with veterinary ophthalmologist Dr. DJ Haeussler for a real clinical conversation about the feline eye cases that challenge general practitioners the most, starting with the corneal ulcer that just won't close. A limping dog walks into your exam room. The owner says it started two weeks ago. The leg looks fine. The X-rays look fine. Nothing adds up — yet. In this episode of Mystery Case Rounds, Dr. Shannon Gregoire walks through a real clinical case of canine lameness from the first exam to the final diagnosis, showing exactly how she thinks through a case when the answer isn't obvious. Veterinary emergency specialist Dr. Kristin Welch walks through a real hyperglycemia case that didn't follow the textbook. Watch the diagnostic reasoning unfold on Vet Candy's Mystery Case Rounds. Dr. Ashley Bourgeois breaks down what is really going on when a Pomeranian loses its coat, the hormonal, genetic, and inflammatory factors may be at play, why this breed is uniquely predisposed to certain dermatologic conditions, and how to build a workup that actually leads somewhere instead of chasing your tail. Nearly a quarter of homeless youth in the U.S. have pets — and some choose veterinary care over their own health care. The Seattle One Health Clinic offers both, side by side, for free. Jeremiah Pouncy shares why this One Health model is changing how we think about the human-animal bond and community care. In Barcelona, scientists are building a biological deep freeze for endangered species, storing genetic material from nearly 300 species and using AI to unlock the future of conservation. Jeremiah Pouncy explains how the Barcelona CryoZoo could change everything we know about saving wildlife from extinction. With fewer than 800 left on Earth, the Bengal florican is one of the rarest birds alive. But in India's Manas National Park, over 800 former poachers have become the species' fiercest protectors. Jeremiah Pouncy tells the remarkable story of how community-led conservation turned a near-extinction into a comeback. A new study on the "Capitoline dolphins" off Rome's coast reveals a population in crisis. Seven out of ten show signs of malnutrition, many bear scars from fishing gear, and scientists warn they may disappear without urgent intervention. Jeremiah Pouncy breaks down what is threatening one of the world's most historically significant dolphin populations and why it matters. Going back to veterinary school usually means new classes, new rotations, new schedules, and the familiar feeling that summer disappeared way too fast. For the hosts of Vet School After Dark , it also means catching up on where everyone spent the break and figuring out how to mentally transition back into another demanding academic year. Vet Candy's hit podcast recently went live in Nashville, and what started as another fast-paced battle of veterinary knowledge quickly turned into something no one in the room saw coming. Dr. Lauren Downey Koos didn't have to look far to get to WVC Nashville. She works at BluePearl Veterinary in Franklin, Tennessee, which means the conference is essentially in her backyard. She graduated from the University of Florida in 2018, went into neurology, and became a specialist faster than most people finish paying off their student loans. Hosts Caitlin and Clay Palme…

records.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, October 22, 2026 FAO: Call to Strengthen Prevention, Surveillance, and Preparedness against HPAI in Latin America and the Caribbean #19,383 Although HPAI H5 has reached nearly every corner of the world, reporting from many regions remains spotty at best. Sometimes this data is deliberately withheld for political or economic reasons, but often it is due to a lack of resources, or difficulties conducting surveillance in remote or uninhabited regions. The FAO's map of 2025-2026 Global AIV activity illustrates these gaps: Large swaths of Asia, Africa, South and Central America, and Northern Canada are essentially a blank slate. Yet we know, based on bird migratory patterns (flyways), that HPAI incursions almost certainly are occurring. Major Global Migratory Flyways – Credit FAO Last week the FAO issued an alert to Latin American and Caribbean nations advising them to strengthen their surveillance for - and preparedness against - HPAI as the coming months are likely to see an increased risk for outbreaks. Due to its length, I've only posted some excerpts. Follow the link to read the document in its entirety. I'll have a brief postscript after the break. CALL TO STRENGTHEN PREVENTION, SURVEILLANCE AND PREPAREDNESS MEASURES AGAINST HIGH PATHOGENICITY AVIAN INFLUENZA IN LATIN AMERICA AND THE CARIBBEAN 16 October 2026 Given the continued circulation of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) viruses in the Americas and the proximity of a period of increased risk associated with the seasonal movements of migratory wild birds from the northern hemisphere to Latin America and the Caribbean, FAO calls on official veterinary services, public health authorities, poultry producers and other stakeholders involved in animal health to strengthen prevention, surveillance, early detection and response preparedness measures against this disease. HPAI continues to pose a health threat to poultry, wildlife and potentially other animal species and people. Avian influenza A(H5) viruses have continued to circulate across the continent in 2026. More than 10 countries in the Americas have reported over 1 000 outbreaks and cases in domestic, wild and mammalian animals, according to data from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and the countries. Experience over the past few years shows that wild birds, particularly migratory waterbirds, can play an important role in the geographical spread of avian influenza viruses. The migration and concentration of birds from different geographical areas provide opportunities for virus circulation and can increase the risk of introduction of the virus into domestic bird populations. According to official WOAH data and analysis of FAO EMPRES-i+ data over the past few years, HPAI outbreaks tend to increase from October and reach their highest levels during the following months. For this reason, the coming period requires increased vigilance and preparedness, especially in countries, territories and areas along migratory routes, in wetlands, lagoons, coastal areas or other places where wild birds congregate, and in areas where poultry farms are located close to these environments. Avian influenza is a highly contagious viral disease that mainly affects domestic and wild birds. However, during the current epidemiological situation, infections have also been identified in various species of terrestrial and marine mammals. In addition, certain avian influenza viruses have zoonotic potential and can occasionally infect humans, mainly in situations of close contact and without adequate protection with infected animals or contaminated environments. Although the risk to the general population is still considered low, surveillance should be maintained, especially among people with occupational or frequent exposure to potentially infected animals (Pan American Health Organization, (Pan American Health Organization, PAHO). Based on the FAO-WOAH Global strategy for the prevention and control of high pathogenicity avian influenza (2024-2033) – Achieving sustainable, resilient poultry production systems, the FAO Regional Office for Latin America and the Caribbean provides specific recommendations for veterinary services and poultry producers. (Continue . . . ) While it is impossible to achieve anything approaching 100% surveillance, the more information we can gather and share, the less likely we are to be blindsided by an abrupt evolutionary change in the virus. But whether that is enough of an incentive to see real change in the amount and quality of global surveillance and reporting on HPAI remains to be seen. CDC COCA Call Today: What Clinicians Need to Know about Dengue in the United States #19,382 Later today (Thursday, Oct 22nd) the CDC will hold a COCA Call for clinicians and other healthcare professionals on this year's record breaking spread of Dengue in Florida (see chart above). Carried and spread by mosquitoes, Dengue fever first returned to Florida in 2009 after an absence of nearly 70 years (see 2010 MMWR report Locally Acquired Dengue --- Key West, Florida, 2009--2010). The virus was likely imported by someone with recent travel to a dengue endemic region who served as a blood meal for a local mosquito, which then began spreading the virus to others. Initially, more than 2 dozen Dengue patients were identified in and around Key West in the fall of 2009, although a year later, the CDC would report far more people were exposed (see CDC Press Release Report Suggests Nearly 5 Percent Exposed to Dengue Virus in Key West). This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded nearly 300 imported cases (see chart below), with the vast majority linked to Cuba. This year's locally acquired outbreak is the largest reported by Florida since the 1940s. While this may seem primarily a `Florida problem' - this is a tourist state - and doctors anywhere in the country (and internationally) could see Dengue cases arising from this outbreak. Accordingly, the CDC will hold a COCA (Clinician Outreach & Communication Activity) call this afternoon. While these presentations are often technical and are of greatest interest to clinicians and healthcare providers, they are usually archived within a few days, and made available to the general public. Details on today's presentation follow: What Clinicians Need to Know about Dengue in the United States For Health Care Providers Oct. 22, 2026, visit link for details. At a glance During this COCA Call, presenters will discuss current dengue epidemiology in the United States and review dengue clinical features, current diagnostic testing recommendations, and clinical management guidelines. Overview Dengue virus is endemic in several U.S. territories and freely associated states and has caused increasing numbers of travel-associated and locally acquired dengue cases in U.S. states in recent years. No preventative medicines or specific antiviral treatments are available for dengue. Severe dengue is a medical emergency—recognition of warning signs and appropriate clinical management are critical for reducing severe outcomes. During this COCA Call, presenters will discuss current dengue epidemiology in the United States and review dengue clinical features, current diagnostic testing recommendations, and clinical management guidelines. Webinar Call Details Date & Time: Thursday, October 22, 2026 - 2:00 – 3:00 PM ET A few minutes before the webinar begins, please click this link to join. Presenters Laura Adams, DVM, MPH, DACVPM Epidemiologist Dengue Branch, Division of Vector-Borne Diseases National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Liliana Sánchez-González, MD, MPH, CTropMed Medical Epidemiologist Dengue Branch, Division of Vector-Borne Diseases National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Call Objectives COCA Call Objectives At the conclusion of the session, the participant will be able to accomplish the following: Cite background information on the topic covered during the presentation. Identify CDC's role in the topic covered during the presentation. Describe the topic's implications for clinicians. Identify concerns and issues related to preparedness for and response to urgent public health threats. Identify how an interprofessional team of healthcare providers can work with patients to promote disease prevention. Activity-specific Objectives At the conclusion of this session, the participant will be able to accomplish the following: Summarize dengue epidemiology and transmission in the United States. List the clinical features of dengue. Explain dengue diagnostic testing for patients with suspected dengue. Describe appropriate treatment for dengue patients according to severity classification. Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping MMWR: Fatal Human Case of HPAI A(H5N5) in a Backyard Flock Owner — Washington, November 2025 #19,381 In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian H5N5; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to an MMWR report - by `early and repeated negative influenza test results from upper respiratory swab specimens'. As we've previously discussed, it takes a certain amount of luck for novel flu infections to be detected, properly treated, and then reported to the CDC. The problem being that standard rapid influenza tests don't distinguish between seasonal and novel flu strains, and sometimes, repeated swabs of the upper airway can fail to `capture' a deep lung infection for RT-PCR testing. In the H5N5 case above, the patient died. In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had H5N1 (see Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri). In both cases, numerous hospital workers (and others) were unknowingly exposed. How many novel flu infections go undetected is unknown, although numerous studies suggest it happens more than we think (see JAMA Open: Asymptomatic Human Infections With Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Confirmed by Molecular and Serologic Testing and MMWR: Serologic Evidence of Recent Infection with HPAI A(H5) Virus Among Dairy Workers). No screening system can be expected to catch every case (and many mild cases simply won't seek medical care), but a standardized screening procedure can improve the chances. Yesterday King County, Washington published updated guidance for screening for novel influenza, following last week's report of a dairy-exposure infection in Yakima county. This appears to be a condensed version of guidance published by the WA State Dept. of Health (Provider Alert: Testing and Subtyping for Avian Influenza) published on Oct 9th. The emphasis here is on testing patients with ARI (Acute Respiratory Illness) with recent (past 10 days) epidemiologic risk factors (poultry/livestock exposure, raw dairy or animal products, known contact with a human case, etc.). It should be noted that this criteria would not have targeted the BC teenager with H5N1, the Missouri case mentioned above, and several others whose source of exposure remains unknown. Credit CDC In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours. Today's guidance appears to back away from that, although the reason behind that isn't stated. Based on the CDC's analysis of 72 human cases since 2024, however, it does appear that the vast majority of known cases had some kind of animal exposure. I've reproduced the King County Guidance below, followed by a link to the WA State provider update. I'll have a postscript after the break. October 20, 2026 Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping ➜ This health advisory is also available in PDF format (223 KB) Current situation Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI or bird flu) continues to circulate among wild birds and other animals in Washington. Although the risk to the general public remains low, clinicians should remain vigilant for possible avian influenza infections in patients with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and epidemiologic risk factors. Guidance has changed for the 2026-27 influenza season, summarized below. Actions requested Identify Test all patients with ARI AND epidemiologic risk factors for influenza and obtain seasonal influenza subtyping for influenza A-positive specimens. Epidemiologic risk factors include the following within 10 days before symptom onset: Close contact with sick or dead animals or their environments, especially birds, wildlife, livestock (including poultry), or domestic animals suspected of HPAI Consumption or handling of raw animal products or parts from potentially infected animals (e.g., raw cow milk or products made with it, raw meat-based pet food) Close contact (within 6 feet) to someone suspected or confirmed to have avian influenza Influenza A subtyping is NOT requested for patients without epidemiologic risk factors, including hospitalized patients. Note this is a change from previous recommendations. Test Avian influenza testing is available at WA DOH Public Health Laboratories (PHL) with prior approval from Public Health. If seasonal influenza A subtyping is not available through a clinical or commercial lab, the following specimens may be submitted directly to PHL without pre-approval: All influenza A specimens that result as "unsubtypeable" (influenza A positive test but seasonal influenza A subtype was negative or not identifiable) Specimens from hospitalized patients with risk factors for avian influenza, when seasonal influenza subtyping is not available Notify Immediately report suspected and confirmed cases of novel influenza to Public Health at 206-296-4774, including patients with ARI and identified epidemiologic risk factors. Do not wait for lab confirmation before notifying us. The following are immediately notifiable: All suspected novel influenza, including avian influenza (influenza A H5 or others); a negative influenza PCR does not rule out avian influenza All influenza A specimens that result as "unsubtypeable" CONTACT Communicable Diseases Epidemiology and Immunization Section 401 5th Ave, Suite 1250 Seattle, WA 98104 Phone: 206-296-4774 TTY Relay: 711 Fax: 206-296-4803 Provider Alert: Testing and Subtyping for Avian Influenza, WA State Dept. of Health Influenza Virus Testing at the Washington State Public Health Laboratories (PHL) including Novel Influenza and Fatal Influenza Influenza Specimen Collection and submission Instructions, WA State Dept. of Health Influenza Specimen Collection, CDC A(H5) Bird Flu: Current Situation | Bird Flu, CDC Three years ago, in UK Novel Flu Surveillance: Quantifying TTD, we looked at a UKHSA report that it would likely take between 3 and 10 weeks before community spread of a novel flu virus would become apparent to authorities, after anywhere between a few dozen to a few thousand community infections In 2024 the ECDC issued guidance for member nations on Enhanced Influenza Surveillance to Detect Avian Influenza Virus Infections in the EU/EEA During the Inter-Seasonal Period., which cautioned: Sentinel surveillance systems are important for the monitoring of respiratory viruses in the EU/EEA, but these systems are not designed and are not sufficiently sensitive to identify a newly emerging virus such as avian influenza in the general population early enough for the purpose of implementing control measures in a timely way. A sobering reminder that, while we comfort ourselves with our current low number of human novel flu detections, we are probably missing some cases. Tuesday, October 20, 2026 Washington State Confirms 5 More Dairy Herds Infected With H5N1 (n=8) Credit Washington State Dept Ag. #19,380 Not quite 2 weeks ago the USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State, which was followed a week later by the first (reportedly mild) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection). Details, such as the genotype, how cattle may have been infected, and the exact exposure (apparently, dairy cattle related) of the human case have yet to be released. On Oct 8th, the USDA stated "APHIS will complete genetic sequencing and announce final results as soon as they are available.", but thus far I've seen nothing published. Screenshot taken today, Oct 20th, 2026. Three days ago I posted Washington State Confirms 3rd Dairy Herd Infected With H5N1, which was apparently reported on the 15th. Yesterday the USDA and Washington State Department of Agriculture added 5 more herds, all reportedly in Yakima County. Other than the above updated dashboards and graphics, I've found no other information on these latest developments. As mentioned previously, Washington is one of the few U.S. states that allows the sale of raw milk in grocery stores, natural food markets, food co-ops, and direct-to-consumer farm stores. While I'm confident that pasteurization effectively kills the H5N1 virus in commercial milk, raw milk (and milk products) are a different matter. In 2024 and 2025 we saw a number of high profile reports of pets infected with H5N1 via raw milk and/or raw pet food (see Washington State (WSDA) Announces 2 Households with H5N1 Infected Cats Linked to Raw Food). On Oct 8th, the State of Washington issued this warning: Dairy product safety Pasteurization inactivates viruses and bacteria in milk, including HPAI virus, helping ensure the safety of the dairy supply. The zoo will remain closed on Oct 22 and 23 Chennai: Seven waterbirds at the Vedanthangal enclosure of Vandalur Zoo died of H5N1 avian influenza, a national laboratory confirmed on Wednesday. The result comes seven months after 40 birds died at Guindy Children’s Park. The zoo will remain closed on Oct 22 and 23.The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD) in Bhopal confirmed the H5N1 avian influenza virus in the birds. “We sent the samples for testing when the birds died. The results were out today. Disinfection measures were taken soon after the deaths were reported. No deaths have been reported since the last death on Oct. 9,” zoo director Ritto Cyriac told TOI, adding that “the outbreak is likely over.”H5N1 is a highly pathogenic strain of avian influenza (bird flu) that spreads mainly among birds, wild and domestic, kills them in large numbers, and can occasionally infect mammals, including humans. Among birds, H5N1 spreads mainly through virus shed in droppings, saliva and nasal secretions. Sick birds often show breathing, eye and nerve problems, or die suddenly.Four painted storks, a pelican grey, a grey heron and a darter died between Oct 3 and Oct 9 in the zoo. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like New SUVs With Tiny Price Tags (Take A Look)SearchResultOffers | Search Ads Learn More Undo The zoo disinfected the area and treated the remaining birds. “Medicines including prophylactic oral antibiotics, herbal antiviral medications, immunostimulants and liver supplements were given to all water birds through fish for seven days. Enclosures were sprayed with an antiviral disinfectant solution. The water inside was disinfected, cleaned, and replaced with fresh water. The affected area was cordoned off with ropes to restrict visitor access,” Cyriac added. The zoo authorities, meanwhile, urged visitors to cooperate with the closure. “This temporary measure is intended to facilitate intensive sanitisation, strengthen biosecurity measures, and ensure close monitoring of the situation,” the zoo said in release. Vandalur Zoo Closes Due to Bird Flu Spread Threat The Vandalur Zoo will not allow visitors on October 22 and 23 as a precautionary measure following confirmation of H5N1 Avian Influenza infection in water birds by NIHSAD on October 21, 2026, the zoo authorities said By : PTI Update: 2026-10-22 10:10 GMT Vandalur Zoo. (Wikimedia Commons) Chennai: The Arignar Anna Zoological Park, familiarly known as the Vandalur Zoo, here, has appealed to the public to abstain from visiting the zoological park for two days from Thursday as a precaution following the confirmation of H5N1 Avian Influenza infection in water birds by the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal. The Vandalur Zoo will not allow visitors on October 22 and 23 as a precautionary measure following confirmation of H5N1 Avian Influenza infection in water birds by NIHSAD on October 21, 2026, the zoo authorities said. Immediate preventive measures, including disinfection, sanitisation, and strict implementation of biosecurity protocols, have been undertaken in accordance with the Government of India's guidelines. "No further bird mortality or sickness has been reported since October 9, 2026. This temporary measure is intended to facilitate intensive sanitisation, strengthen biosecurity measures, and ensure close monitoring of the situation. The public is requested to cooperate with the precautionary measures," a statement from the Director of AAZP said on Wednesday. According to sources, seven water birds died in the zoo's largest enclosure - the Vedanthangal birds enclosure - between October 3 and October 9. The fatalities included four painted storks, one grey pelican, one grey heron, and one oriental darter. The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases had confirmed the H5N1 infection from sample testing. Since the situation has remained stable so far, the officials believe the immediate outbreak may already be over. Nevertheless, the temporary two-day closure is being used to carry out intensive sanitisation and disinfection. The area was cordoned off immediately after the first death, and the zoo has intensified biosecurity protocols to ensure the safety of its remaining animals and staff. records.content: BARRON COUNTY, Wis. — Two Barron County commercial poultry flocks have been found to be infected with highly pathogenic avian influenza this week. The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection identified one case on Oct. 19. DATCP said there were 41,417 birds in that flock. DATCP identified another case in a different flock on Oct. 22, with 13,463 birds. This marked the third case of avian flu in Barron County this year. The first was reported Sept. 14, in a flock of 79,088 birds. This also marks the eighth case of bird flu in a commercial or backyard flock this year in the Badger State. Jefferson County saw two cases in commercial farms, and Walworth County saw one in a commercial farm. Racine and Dane counties also had cases in backyard flocks. Both recently affected Barron County farms have had their birds depopulated to prevent the disease from spreading. DATCP said the birds will not enter the food system. Both farms have also been quarantined, per DATCP. The highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, is highly contagious. It’s caused by influenza type A viruses. While HPAI can fluctuate in severity, it is often deadly to domestic poultry. It can spread when coming into contact with an infected bird, being around wild birds or being in contact with bird droppings, clothing worn by someone working with animals or equipment used with animals. The bird flu has been moving throughout the U.S. since Dec. 2021. Aly Prouty - Digital Media Producer Aly Prouty is a digital producer for Spectrum News 1 Wisconsin, Ohio and Kentucky. An award-winning, multimedia journalist, she holds an honors B.A. in journalism from Marquette University and an M.A. in journalism and media studies from The University of Alabama

Additionally, multiple blue-wing teal in Greene County were confirmed to have HPAI through surveillance conducted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services and DNR Division of Fish, Wildlife & Nature Preserves. If you find wild waterfowl or raptors that are dead for no obvious reason or showing any of the following signs of illness, report it online at on.IN.gov/sickwildlife. Signs of HPAI in waterfowl and raptors include: Sudden death. Neurological impairment (e.g., lack of coordination, swimming or walking in circles, tremors, twisted neck). Lack of energy and appetite. Swelling of the head, neck, and eyes. Nasal discharge, cough, sneezing, lack of coordination, and diarrhea. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the public health risk for HPAI is low. However, it is possible for humans to contract the disease. Members of the public should avoid contact with sick waterfowl and other sick wildlife whenever possible. If a carcass must be handled, wear disposable gloves and a mask, double-bag the carcass, and place it in the trash. Wash hands with soap and warm water immediately afterward. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommends that waterfowl hunters wear protective clothing such as face masks and gloves to process birds, and to do so in a well-ventilated area or outdoors. Meat harvested from waterfowl should be cooked to an internal temperature of 165°F before consumption. Please contact the Indiana Department of Health if you develop any of the following symptoms after touching or handling sick or dead waterfowl: fever, chills, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, shortness of breath, eye irritation or redness, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headaches, diarrhea, nausea or vomiting, or rash. Indiana’s Health Department can be reached at 317-233-7125 during regular business hours, or at 317-233-1325 after hours. Follow the prompts in the automated menu to speak to the epidemiologist on call. Some domestic and agricultural animals are also known to be susceptible to HPAI, including poultry, cattle, and cats. If you have these animals at home, be sure to process any harvested waterfowl away from your animals and practice good biosecurity measures. For more information on HPAI and to track suspected cases across the state, visit on.IN.gov/avian-flu. For more information about poultry biosecurity measures, visit aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/defend-the-flock. For those who see any of their poultry acting sick or find any dead, please report it to the Board of Animal Health at IN.gov/boah/species-information/avianbirds/small-flock-and-exhibition-poultry/sick-andor-dead-poultry-questionnaire. The virus spread rapidly across the continent, propelled largely by infection and migration in wild waterfowl. As of August 2026, more than 18,500 individual wild birds from over 170 species have been confirmed positive for the virus in the United States alone. Yet the toll has been strikingly uneven: some dabbling ducks carry the virus without visible illness, while sea ducks, diving ducks, and certain geese have suffered mass mortality events. Understanding why some species weather the panzootic while others collapse has become a central question for wildlife disease ecologists. A new study led by researchers from the U.S. Geological Survey, the University of Georgia’s Southeastern Cooperative Wildlife Disease Study, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and the California Waterfowl Association offers a detailed portrait of infection and immunity in the waterfowl and waterbirds of northern California’s Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge Complex (SNWRC). Published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology, the research leveraged ongoing capture efforts for movement ecology studies between October 2022 and July 2025 to sample wild birds for both active viral infection and serological evidence of previous exposure. The results reveal a population largely carrying the immunological fingerprints of H5N1 exposure, alongside surprising evidence that some sympatric waterbird species may be far less engaged with the virus than their duck and goose neighbors. Find Treatments Discover more Shop Bird Supplies Find Treatments Try Science Kits The SNWRC spans roughly 70,000 acres of managed wetlands in the Sacramento Valley and serves as critical habitat for migratory and wintering waterfowl in the Pacific Flyway. Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge alone has historically hosted an estimated 16 percent of California’s wintering ducks, or 10 to 15 percent of the Pacific Flyway’s population. This extraordinary density of birds makes the complex a natural laboratory for avian influenza surveillance—and a place where the consequences of HPAI incursion have been painfully visible. A mortality event from June 2022 through January 2023 killed an estimated 100 Snow Geese, with smaller losses among Mallards, Gadwall, Canada Geese, and even American White Pelicans. A subsequent outbreak from December 2023 through January 2024 killed over 1,100 Snow Geese and 200 Ross’s Geese. Beyond mortality, some infected Snow Geese have failed to migrate or delayed their departure, extending the ecological footprint of the virus. Book a Safari Discover more Check Symptoms Get Cold Relief Study Biology infections Between October 2022 and July 2025, the team captured assorted waterbirds—ducks, geese, coots, and stilts—using rocket nets and air boats with dip nets during targeted sampling windows in July, October, and December. Each bird received a federal metal band, and paired oropharyngeal and cloacal swabs were collected using sterile polyester-tipped applicators and placed in cold virus transport medium. When study parameters allowed, blood was drawn from the jugular vein, centrifuged to separate serum, and archived for antibody testing. All birds appeared healthy at the time of processing, with no clinical signs typical of HPAI infection. Laboratory work proceeded on two fronts: viral RNA was extracted from swabs and screened by real-time reverse transcriptase PCR targeting the influenza A virus matrix gene and the clade 2.3.4.4b H5 hemagglutinin, while serum samples were heat-inactivated and tested with a commercial blocking enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (bELISA) for antibodies to influenza A viruses (IAVs). The scale of the effort was substantial: 384 swab samples and 204 sera from assorted waterfowl and waterbird species were analyzed. Yet active HPAI H5N1 infection was confirmed in only three individuals—two Snow Geese and one Greater White-fronted Goose—all asymptomatic at capture. The National Veterinary Services Laboratory confirmed all three detections as clade 2.3.4.4b HPAI H5N1. A B3.6 genotype virus was isolated from the Greater White-fronted Goose sample, while the Snow Goose samples failed to meet the cycle threshold at which virus isolation is attempted. The near absence of detectable infection across three years of sampling, in a refuge that has experienced repeated HPAI mortality events, immediately raised the question of what the serological data might explain. Book a Safari Discover more Read Med Journals Track Outbreaks Book a Safari The antibody results were striking. Of 164 waterfowl tested, 107 (65 percent) tested positive for antibodies to IAVs; among 40 additional waterbirds, 12 (30 percent) were positive. Antibodies were detected in all duck and goose species sampled, and the majority of positive samples also carried antibodies specific to both the H5 hemagglutinin and the N1 neuraminidase—the two surface proteins of the circulating H5N1 strain. In ducks sampled during October, the proportion of IAV antibody-positive birds carrying both H5 and N1 antibodies remained high and relatively constant, at 64 percent in 2023 and 80 percent in 2024. A remarkable 88 percent of ducks sampled in July 2025 also carried antibodies to both proteins. This pattern indicates a population-level history of substantial exposure to H5N1 and subsequent survival, consistent with findings from numerous duck species in the Mississippi Flyway, where H5 and N1 antibodies increased dramatically following the 2.3.4.4b incursion. Book a Safari The study also reports the first known observation of H5 antibodies in the American Coot (Fulica americana), a waterbird species not traditionally associated with influenza A virus circulation. However, both overall IAV seroprevalence and H5-specific antibodies in coots were notably lower than in sympatric waterfowl: IAV antibody prevalence fell from 54 percent in 2023 to 24 percent in 2024, and only 14 to 20 percent of antibody-positive coots carried both H5 and N1 antibodies. Black-necked Stilts showed similarly minimal antibody detection, though sampling was especially limited for this species. The disparity between coots and the ducks and geese sharing the same aquatic habitats cannot be directly explained by the data, but the authors suggest two possibilities: coots may have lower innate susceptibility to infection, or they may exhibit behaviors that limit exposure. A survivorship bias—in which most exposed individuals died—seems unlikely given the low number of American Coot mortalities reported during the outbreak. Get Cold Relief Translating antibody prevalence into population immunity is complicated, but experimental studies offer a framework. Sequential challenges with low pathogenic (LP) and highly pathogenic (HP) IAVs have shown that previous exposure can reduce infection, mortality, and viral shedding during subsequent infections with both LP and HP H5 viruses. The relatively high level of subtype-specific immunity observed in ducks—up to 80 percent carrying both H5 and N1 antibodies—may partially explain the near absence of detectable HPAI H5N1 infection during the study years. The authors caution, however, that the serologic techniques used cannot determine whether H5 or N1 antibodies result solely from HP H5N1 exposure; they likely represent a history of exposure to both HP and LP H5 viruses, and LP H5 viruses are known to circulate commonly in these wetlands, potentially maintained locally by non-migratory waterfowl. Cross-reactive antibodies and antigenic imprinting may also mask antigenic differences between LP and HP H5 viruses, preventing definitive estimation of specific exposure history. The findings also validate the bELISA screening threshold used in the study. A serum-to-negative control absorbance ratio below 0.7 proved an effective guide for further serotyping: while some individuals above the threshold tested positive for H5 and N1 antibodies, this represented only a small percentage of samples. The authors note that test sensitivity may vary over time and among testing formats, and that the timing of infection before sampling cannot be known, but the threshold should not introduce significant error in detecting subtype-specific antibodies. This methodological validation matters for surveillance programs considering serology as a complementary tool to the U.S. national active surveillance strategy, which focuses on viral detection in waterfowl and does not include species such as coots. Overall, the study underscores the value of serologic surveillance as a supportive strategy for informing HPAI H5N1 risk management in wild birds. The high level of IAV immunity in waterfowl suggests, based on experimental evidence, a reduced potential for widespread or seasonally concentrated mortality in these populations. Results from coots and stilts highlight the species differences that exist in exposure and potential risk at a given site and time—and the possibility that some species remain essentially immunologically naïve and susceptible, even when the virus circulates intensively among sympatric waterfowl. The authors emphasize that additional sampling across subsequent seasons is needed to understand how these immunological baselines shift, but the data provide a critical portrait of the years immediately following the clade 2.3.4.4b incursion in the Pacific Flyway. As HPAI H5N1 continues to evolve and expand its host range across North America, studies like this one—integrating virology, serology, and ecology in a single surveillance framework—will be essential for anticipating where the virus will strike next and which species will bear the burden. records.content: 顶部 首页 首页 隐私 【前沿进展】南极极地病毒研究:H5N1禽流感与企鹅病毒组特征解析 病毒学界 深入探索 体验极速搜索 军事动态 娱乐新闻 广袤的南极大陆,依托南大洋形成天然地理阻隔,长期被视作相对隔绝的生态净土。但随着候鸟迁徙、气候变化与人类活动加剧,外来病原体正不断侵入南极生态系统。高致病性禽流感H5N1(2.3.4.4b分支)在全球广泛流行,该病毒是否入侵南极、当地感染现状如何,一直是全球病毒学界高度关注的重大风险问题。 成果一:HPAI H5N1经候鸟媒介从南美洲传入南极菲尔德斯半岛,毒株NA茎区存在独特17个氨基酸缺失 第一篇研究题为Transcontinental Spread of HPAI H5N1 from South America to Antarctica via Avian Vectors。科考队员在长城站所在的菲尔德斯半岛开展野生动物病原采样,首次在该地区褐贼鸥(brown skua)样本中检出H5N1高致病性禽流感病毒阳性。 2024年12月,科考人员发现一只行为异常、丧失飞行能力的患病褐贼鸥,该个体随后死亡,研究团队采集其肺、脑干组织;后续另采集3只贼鸥组织样本及野外粪便样本。经实时荧光RT-PCR筛查,共获得4份H5N1阳性样本,完成病毒全基因组测序并提交GISAID数据库。 展开剩余 74 % 系统发育与时空谱系地理分析发现,本次南极分离的H5N1属于2.3.4.4b基因型,毒株全部8个基因片段均与南美洲秘鲁、智利流行毒株亲缘关系最近;传播路径重建结果提示,病毒起源于秘鲁,经智利,依靠候鸟迁徙传入南极半岛,褐贼鸥作为迁徙海鸟充当跨大洋传播载体。毒株神经氨酸酶NA茎区出现独特的17个氨基酸缺失(58-74位)。该缺失在全球其他 2.3.4.4b毒株中十分罕见,仅在南极禽类分离株中检出,提示该突变是H5N1进入南极环境后产生的适应性突变。 研究表明,即便南极拥有天然地理屏障,迁徙海鸟仍可充当传播桥梁,将南美洲流行的H5N1引入南极。南极聚集大量高度易感海鸟与海洋哺乳动物,一旦病毒在当地建立持续传播循环,将对极地独特生态系统造成严重威胁。研究呼吁全球强化南极野生动物病原的持续性监测。 图1:系统发育不一致性分析 成果二:阿德利岛三种同域企鹅粪便病毒组均检出多种潜在病毒病原,且宿主物种对病毒群落影响有限 第二篇论文题为Faecal Viromes of Three Sympatric Penguins on Ardley Island, Antarctica: A Tranomic Study Showing Limited HostSpecies Effect。科考团队在紧邻长城站的阿德利岛,采集阿德利企鹅、帽带企鹅、巴布亚企鹅共32份新鲜粪便样本,利用转录组测序解析企鹅肠道病毒组全貌。 研究发现α多样性(物种丰富度、香农指数)在三种企鹅之间无统计学差异;β 多样性分析显示,宿主物种虽然对病毒群落存在统计学影响,但决定系数很低(R2=0.097),宿主物种对病毒组的塑造作用十分微弱。个体差异、食物来源、环境暴露与随机生态过程才是驱动企鹅肠道病毒群落变化的主要因素。 通过二代测序拼接得到多种潜在病原近完整基因组。其中,首次在阿德利企鹅中检出德尔塔冠状病毒,与南极鞘嘴鸥、巴布亚企鹅的德尔塔冠状病毒高度同源, 提示冠状病毒可在南极不同海鸟间跨物种传播,并形成南极本地独立演化谱系。新型星状病毒(Penguin astrovirus 2025):ORF1b(RdRp)、ORF2(衣壳蛋白)序列均低于现有物种划分阈值,判定为新型星状病毒。 虽然本次检出的病毒大多以潜伏、无症状感染为主,但外来病原体进入南极生态系统后,有可能发生适应性突变,提升毒力与跨宿主传播能力;企鹅高密度繁殖群落会进一步加速病毒扩散。该研究构建了南极阿德利岛企鹅病毒组基线数据集,为极地野生动物病毒溢出风险评估提供重要参考依据。 图2:阿德利企鹅、巴布亚企鹅和帽带企鹅的采样地点。 图3:三种同域分布的企鹅物种粪便样本中病毒群落的组成与多样性。 图4:基于ORF2衣壳蛋白和ORF1b RdRp序列的企鹅星状病毒2025序列一致性热图。 论文链接: Free web novels for online reading. 深入探索 财经分析 订阅时事资讯 新闻 评论 全部 还没有人评论过,快来抢首评 抢首评 推荐阅读 南京籍留学生在国外披旭日旗 南京警方回应:有专门部门处理,“这不是小事” 有料新语 前天09:35 169.5万+ 深入探索 The Indiana Department of Natural Resources has confirmed cases of Avian Influenza in Greene and Hamilton County, according to a press release. The department verified that highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) was the cause of death for several geese in Hamilton County. Multiple blue-wing teals have been confirmed to have HPAI in Greene County. Eli Fleace, Fish and Wildlife Health Biologist, says that birds with a developed infection will display strange behavior, which is a strong warning sign. “A lot of times, I will see geese or ducks swimming in really tight concentric circles over and over again.” Fleace said, “A very common sign of avian influenza is [the] seizing or shaking of the head and neck of the bird.” Positive cases have also been reported in Allen and Johnson County since the press release was published, Fleace says. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the public health risk for humans is very low. Fleace advises that the public report any sick or dead wildlife to the DNR’s reporting page. Since the beginning of this year, there have been 2,101 suspected and confirmed cases in wild birds. Of those, 1,923 are confirmed deaths from Bird Flu. Roy Graber October 21, 2026 digicomphoto | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been confirmed in three commercial poultry flocks across North America, with one case in Wisconsin's Barron County and two cases in Alberta, Canada. Affected premises have been quarantined and birds depopulated to prevent further disease spread. One HPAI case confirmed in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County, Wisconsin on October 19, 2024 Two additional HPAI cases reported in Alberta, Canada on October 20, 2024 in Northern Lights County and Foothills County Affected premises have been quarantined and birds depopulated to prevent disease transmission Alberta has now experienced 10 commercial poultry flock losses to HPAI in 2024 At least three new cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) have been confirmed in North America – with one of those in the United States and two in Canada. More specifically, one flock infection has been reported in Wisconsin, while both Canadian cases were in Alberta. Avian influenza in Wisconsin On Oct. 19, the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture , Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) had identified a case of HPAI in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. DATCP stated that its animal health officials were working with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) in a joint incident response. The affected premises has been quarantined to restrict movement of poultry and poultry products. Birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. The state agency did not offer more specific information concerning the type of commercial poultry involved, or how many birds were in the flock. Those numbers are typically released by the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), but the APHIS website that lists that information has not been functional this week, displaying a message that says “publicdashboards.dl.usda.gov’s server IP address could not be found.” Another case of HPAI in Barron County was reported by DATCP and APHIS in September. In that situation, 79,100 commercial meat turkeys were involved. Prior to that, Wisconsin had not had any cases of HPAI since March. Avian influenza in Alberta The Canadian Food Inspection Agency reported that the presence of HPAI was confirmed in two poultry flocks in Alberta on Oct. 20. One was in Northern Lights County and the other was in Foothills County. Further information about these two flocks has not yet been released. To learn more about HPAI cases in commercial poultry flocks in the United States, Mexico and Canada, see an interactive map on WATTPoultry.com.
