records.content_title: Vandalur zoo shuts for two days after seven water birds test positive for H5N1
records.content: Chennai Vandalur zoo shuts for two days after seven water birds test positive for H5N1 Avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, is a viral infection that primarily affects birds. CHENNAI: Arignar Anna Zoological Park in Vandalur will remain closed to visitors on October 22 and 23 following confirmation of H5N1 avian influenza infection in water birds at the zoo by the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, on Wednesday. The zoo reported the deaths of seven water birds between October 3 and 9, including four painted storks, one grey pelican, one grey heron and one darter. The carcasses were found in the largest and most popular Vedanthangal bird's enclosure, which has around 150 birds of 10 different species. "There had been no further bird deaths or reports of sickness since October 9, indicating that the situation had remained stable for the past 12 days. We received confirmation of H5N1 infection on Wednesday and have decided to close the zoo for two days as a precautionary measure,” Zoo director T Ritto Cyriac told the TNIE. The zoo has initiated preventive measures, including disinfection and sanitisation, and is strictly implementing biosecurity protocols in accordance with the Union government's guidelines. The temporary closure will allow officials to intensify sanitisation, strengthen containment measures and closely monitor the health of birds. "As part of preventive measures soon after the deaths were reported, we administered prophylactic oral antibiotics, herbal antiviral medications, immunostimulants and liver supplements to the water birds through fish for seven days. All water bird enclosures were sprayed with an antiviral disinfectant solution. The water in the affected enclosure was disinfected, cleaned and replaced with fresh water. The area was also cordoned off with ropes to restrict visitor access and prevent close proximity to the birds," Ritto explained. Avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, is a viral infection that primarily affects birds. Certain strains, including H5N1, can occasionally infect humans, making precautions and the prevention of exposure to infected birds important. Officials will continue to monitor the birds for any further signs of illness or mortality. The health department is also expected to be involved in the response, with further precautions likely to be taken in coordination with the relevant authorities. The zoo administration said the closure was a precautionary step to protect the bird population and ensure the safety of visitors and staff. Visitors have been requested to cooperate with the temporary restrictions while sanitisation and monitoring measures are carried out. The New Indian Express www.newindianexpress.com

records.content: News World Australia confirms H5N1 on Macquarie Island — The Express Tribune UA.NEWS 17 October 2026 12:52 Australia has confirmed the first case of highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu on the sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island. The virus was detected in samples taken from a southern elephant seal and a kelp gull. First H5 case on the island Australia's Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said official testing had confirmed the presence of the highly pathogenic strain. This is the first recorded H5 case on Macquarie Island, The Express Tribune reports . Macquarie Island is located in the Southern Ocean approximately halfway between the Australian state of Tasmania and Antarctica. The territory is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is an important breeding ground for southern elephant seals. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Risk to the elephant seal population Southern elephant seals can weigh up to 3,600 kilograms and are particularly vulnerable to H5 influenza. According to the federal government, pup mortality in some cases exceeded 90%. At the end of 2025, the virus was recorded in another Australian sub-Antarctic territory — Heard Island. According to local media, more than 13,000 seal pups died there from the infection. In August, Australia's environment ministry reported withdrawing personnel from the research station on Macquarie due to the psychosocial risk to expedition members in the event of an H5 outbreak. Expert assessments had projected significant mortality among elephant seals during the next breeding season. Read us on Download our app

Check out the Fetch On-Demand Catalog| Veterinary Podcast Advertisement News|Articles|October 20, 2026 Avian flu was primary cause of death for Big Bear bald eagle Jackie, necropsy findings show Author(s)Abi Bautista-Alejandre, Assistant Editor Fact checked by: Yasmeen Qahwash An atypical presentation of the virus led to internal bleeding, anemia, and sepsis in the famous bald eagle whose illness had puzzled her care team for weeks. Advertisement Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) was the primary underlying cause of death for Jackie, a bald eagle known to viewers of a livestream from Big Bear Valley in California, according to necropsy and diagnostic findings released October 14 by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).1 For more than a decade, viewers around the world followed Jackie and her mate, Shadow, as they nested and raised eaglets. Jackie, who was about 14 years old, died in August after weeks of treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center in California. She had been treated for several health problems, including anemia. After her death, veterinary pathologists at San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance performed a necropsy, followed by additional laboratory and toxicology testing, according to CDFW.1 “Jackie's necropsy confirmed...HPAI as the primary underlying cause of her decline,” Steven Kubiski, DVM, PhD, DACVP, director of disease investigations at the alliance, said in a statement released by CDFW. The infection caused an unusual complication: a severe stomach ulcer that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and bacterial sepsis, he said.1 A stomach ulcer led to further complications Pathologists found chronic disease in Jackie's ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach commonly known as the gizzard. The ulcerated tissue caused ongoing blood loss and severe anemia and provided a pathway for bacteria to enter her body, resulting in a secondary infection, according to CDFW. Testing also revealed severe inflammation and blood clots in her heart and several major blood vessels. HPAI genetic material was detected in multiple tissues, including the ulcerated ventriculus.1 Additional testing ruled out West Nile virus. Heavy metal levels, including lead, were within acceptable limits and were not considered a factor in the progression of her illness, CDFW said. Toxicology screening detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in Jackie's liver, along with persistent environmental contaminants. However, the necropsy did not reveal the uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with anticoagulant rodenticide exposure. CDFW therefore did not identify brodifacoum as the primary cause of her illness or death. The US Department of Agriculture National Veterinary Services Laboratories provided final confirmation of the HPAI infection, according to the agency. Advertisement CDFW said the findings indicated that several severe, interconnected disease processes developed over time and ultimately led to Jackie's death. The diagnosis was unexpected During Jackie's hospitalization, clinicians at the Ojai Raptor Center investigated several possible causes of her illness, including lead poisoning, zinc toxicity, rodenticide poisoning, and cancer. She also received a blood transfusion, USA Today reported.2 The HPAI diagnosis came as a surprise because Jackie did not exhibit the clinical signs typically associated with the infection in eagles, and no active outbreak had been reported in the area, William Bowerman, a professor of wildlife ecology and environmental toxicology at the University of Maryland, told USA Today.2 Chris Eksteen, MEd, executive director of the Ojai Raptor Center, said the necropsy findings helped explain observations the team made during Jackie's treatment, according to the CDFW release.1 HPAI continues to circulate among wild birds HPAI continues to circulate in wild bird populations across the United States, according to CDFW. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of avian influenza viruses, whereas eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating infected prey, the agency said.1 Bald eagles feed largely on fish and waterfowl. Waterfowl can carry avian influenza viruses without showing signs of illness, increasing the risk that predators will consume infected birds, according to the National Park Service. Eagles may also eat sick birds or recently dead carcasses, providing another route of exposure.3 The US Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository cremated Jackie's remains under established procedures intended to prevent the spread of HPAI to wildlife and humans. CDFW said camera footage provided no evidence that Shadow or the pair's eaglets were ill.1 “Jackie’s death also marked the loss of one half of the iconic bald eagle pair that has occupied Big Bear Valley for years. Her mate, Shadow, remains in Big Bear. Based on camera data, we have no evidence that Shadow or the eaglets were sick,” CDFW wrote in its announcement.1 The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015. Bald eagle populations in the United States rebounded after the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were implemented, allowing the species to be removed from the federal endangered species list.4 References Necropsy provides new information about beloved bald eagle known as Jackie. records.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, October 22, 2026 FAO: Call to Strengthen Prevention, Surveillance, and Preparedness against HPAI in Latin America and the Caribbean #19,383 Although HPAI H5 has reached nearly every corner of the world, reporting from many regions remains spotty at best. Sometimes this data is deliberately withheld for political or economic reasons, but often it is due to a lack of resources, or difficulties conducting surveillance in remote or uninhabited regions. The FAO's map of 2025-2026 Global AIV activity illustrates these gaps: Large swaths of Asia, Africa, South and Central America, and Northern Canada are essentially a blank slate. Yet we know, based on bird migratory patterns (flyways), that HPAI incursions almost certainly are occurring. Major Global Migratory Flyways – Credit FAO Last week the FAO issued an alert to Latin American and Caribbean nations advising them to strengthen their surveillance for - and preparedness against - HPAI as the coming months are likely to see an increased risk for outbreaks. Due to its length, I've only posted some excerpts. Follow the link to read the document in its entirety. I'll have a brief postscript after the break. CALL TO STRENGTHEN PREVENTION, SURVEILLANCE AND PREPAREDNESS MEASURES AGAINST HIGH PATHOGENICITY AVIAN INFLUENZA IN LATIN AMERICA AND THE CARIBBEAN 16 October 2026 Given the continued circulation of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) viruses in the Americas and the proximity of a period of increased risk associated with the seasonal movements of migratory wild birds from the northern hemisphere to Latin America and the Caribbean, FAO calls on official veterinary services, public health authorities, poultry producers and other stakeholders involved in animal health to strengthen prevention, surveillance, early detection and response preparedness measures against this disease. HPAI continues to pose a health threat to poultry, wildlife and potentially other animal species and people. Avian influenza A(H5) viruses have continued to circulate across the continent in 2026. More than 10 countries in the Americas have reported over 1 000 outbreaks and cases in domestic, wild and mammalian animals, according to data from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and the countries. Experience over the past few years shows that wild birds, particularly migratory waterbirds, can play an important role in the geographical spread of avian influenza viruses. The migration and concentration of birds from different geographical areas provide opportunities for virus circulation and can increase the risk of introduction of the virus into domestic bird populations. According to official WOAH data and analysis of FAO EMPRES-i+ data over the past few years, HPAI outbreaks tend to increase from October and reach their highest levels during the following months. For this reason, the coming period requires increased vigilance and preparedness, especially in countries, territories and areas along migratory routes, in wetlands, lagoons, coastal areas or other places where wild birds congregate, and in areas where poultry farms are located close to these environments. Avian influenza is a highly contagious viral disease that mainly affects domestic and wild birds. However, during the current epidemiological situation, infections have also been identified in various species of terrestrial and marine mammals. In addition, certain avian influenza viruses have zoonotic potential and can occasionally infect humans, mainly in situations of close contact and without adequate protection with infected animals or contaminated environments. Although the risk to the general population is still considered low, surveillance should be maintained, especially among people with occupational or frequent exposure to potentially infected animals (Pan American Health Organization, (Pan American Health Organization, PAHO). Based on the FAO-WOAH Global strategy for the prevention and control of high pathogenicity avian influenza (2024-2033) – Achieving sustainable, resilient poultry production systems, the FAO Regional Office for Latin America and the Caribbean provides specific recommendations for veterinary services and poultry producers. (Continue . . . ) While it is impossible to achieve anything approaching 100% surveillance, the more information we can gather and share, the less likely we are to be blindsided by an abrupt evolutionary change in the virus. But whether that is enough of an incentive to see real change in the amount and quality of global surveillance and reporting on HPAI remains to be seen. CDC COCA Call Today: What Clinicians Need to Know about Dengue in the United States #19,382 Later today (Thursday, Oct 22nd) the CDC will hold a COCA Call for clinicians and other healthcare professionals on this year's record breaking spread of Dengue in Florida (see chart above). Carried and spread by mosquitoes, Dengue fever first returned to Florida in 2009 after an absence of nearly 70 years (see 2010 MMWR report Locally Acquired Dengue --- Key West, Florida, 2009--2010). The virus was likely imported by someone with recent travel to a dengue endemic region who served as a blood meal for a local mosquito, which then began spreading the virus to others. Initially, more than 2 dozen Dengue patients were identified in and around Key West in the fall of 2009, although a year later, the CDC would report far more people were exposed (see CDC Press Release Report Suggests Nearly 5 Percent Exposed to Dengue Virus in Key West). This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded nearly 300 imported cases (see chart below), with the vast majority linked to Cuba. This year's locally acquired outbreak is the largest reported by Florida since the 1940s. While this may seem primarily a `Florida problem' - this is a tourist state - and doctors anywhere in the country (and internationally) could see Dengue cases arising from this outbreak. Accordingly, the CDC will hold a COCA (Clinician Outreach & Communication Activity) call this afternoon. While these presentations are often technical and are of greatest interest to clinicians and healthcare providers, they are usually archived within a few days, and made available to the general public. Details on today's presentation follow: What Clinicians Need to Know about Dengue in the United States For Health Care Providers Oct. 22, 2026, visit link for details. At a glance During this COCA Call, presenters will discuss current dengue epidemiology in the United States and review dengue clinical features, current diagnostic testing recommendations, and clinical management guidelines. Overview Dengue virus is endemic in several U.S. territories and freely associated states and has caused increasing numbers of travel-associated and locally acquired dengue cases in U.S. states in recent years. No preventative medicines or specific antiviral treatments are available for dengue. Severe dengue is a medical emergency—recognition of warning signs and appropriate clinical management are critical for reducing severe outcomes. During this COCA Call, presenters will discuss current dengue epidemiology in the United States and review dengue clinical features, current diagnostic testing recommendations, and clinical management guidelines. Webinar Call Details Date & Time: Thursday, October 22, 2026 - 2:00 – 3:00 PM ET A few minutes before the webinar begins, please click this link to join. Presenters Laura Adams, DVM, MPH, DACVPM Epidemiologist Dengue Branch, Division of Vector-Borne Diseases National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Liliana Sánchez-González, MD, MPH, CTropMed Medical Epidemiologist Dengue Branch, Division of Vector-Borne Diseases National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Call Objectives COCA Call Objectives At the conclusion of the session, the participant will be able to accomplish the following: Cite background information on the topic covered during the presentation. Identify CDC's role in the topic covered during the presentation. Describe the topic's implications for clinicians. Identify concerns and issues related to preparedness for and response to urgent public health threats. Identify how an interprofessional team of healthcare providers can work with patients to promote disease prevention. Activity-specific Objectives At the conclusion of this session, the participant will be able to accomplish the following: Summarize dengue epidemiology and transmission in the United States. List the clinical features of dengue. Explain dengue diagnostic testing for patients with suspected dengue. Describe appropriate treatment for dengue patients according to severity classification. Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping MMWR: Fatal Human Case of HPAI A(H5N5) in a Backyard Flock Owner — Washington, November 2025 #19,381 In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian H5N5; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to an MMWR report - by `early and repeated negative influenza test results from upper respiratory swab specimens'. As we've previously discussed, it takes a certain amount of luck for novel flu infections to be detected, properly treated, and then reported to the CDC. The problem being that standard rapid influenza tests don't distinguish between seasonal and novel flu strains, and sometimes, repeated swabs of the upper airway can fail to `capture' a deep lung infection for RT-PCR testing. In the H5N5 case above, the patient died. In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had H5N1 (see Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri). In both cases, numerous hospital workers (and others) were unknowingly exposed. How many novel flu infections go undetected is unknown, although numerous studies suggest it happens more than we think (see JAMA Open: Asymptomatic Human Infections With Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Confirmed by Molecular and Serologic Testing and MMWR: Serologic Evidence of Recent Infection with HPAI A(H5) Virus Among Dairy Workers). No screening system can be expected to catch every case (and many mild cases simply won't seek medical care), but a standardized screening procedure can improve the chances. Yesterday King County, Washington published updated guidance for screening for novel influenza, following last week's report of a dairy-exposure infection in Yakima county. This appears to be a condensed version of guidance published by the WA State Dept. of Health (Provider Alert: Testing and Subtyping for Avian Influenza) published on Oct 9th. The emphasis here is on testing patients with ARI (Acute Respiratory Illness) with recent (past 10 days) epidemiologic risk factors (poultry/livestock exposure, raw dairy or animal products, known contact with a human case, etc.). It should be noted that this criteria would not have targeted the BC teenager with H5N1, the Missouri case mentioned above, and several others whose source of exposure remains unknown. Credit CDC In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours. Today's guidance appears to back away from that, although the reason behind that isn't stated. Based on the CDC's analysis of 72 human cases since 2024, however, it does appear that the vast majority of known cases had some kind of animal exposure. I've reproduced the King County Guidance below, followed by a link to the WA State provider update. I'll have a postscript after the break. October 20, 2026 Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping ➜ This health advisory is also available in PDF format (223 KB) Current situation Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI or bird flu) continues to circulate among wild birds and other animals in Washington. Although the risk to the general public remains low, clinicians should remain vigilant for possible avian influenza infections in patients with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and epidemiologic risk factors. Guidance has changed for the 2026-27 influenza season, summarized below. Actions requested Identify Test all patients with ARI AND epidemiologic risk factors for influenza and obtain seasonal influenza subtyping for influenza A-positive specimens. Epidemiologic risk factors include the following within 10 days before symptom onset: Close contact with sick or dead animals or their environments, especially birds, wildlife, livestock (including poultry), or domestic animals suspected of HPAI Consumption or handling of raw animal products or parts from potentially infected animals (e.g., raw cow milk or products made with it, raw meat-based pet food) Close contact (within 6 feet) to someone suspected or confirmed to have avian influenza Influenza A subtyping is NOT requested for patients without epidemiologic risk factors, including hospitalized patients. Note this is a change from previous recommendations. Test Avian influenza testing is available at WA DOH Public Health Laboratories (PHL) with prior approval from Public Health. If seasonal influenza A subtyping is not available through a clinical or commercial lab, the following specimens may be submitted directly to PHL without pre-approval: All influenza A specimens that result as "unsubtypeable" (influenza A positive test but seasonal influenza A subtype was negative or not identifiable) Specimens from hospitalized patients with risk factors for avian influenza, when seasonal influenza subtyping is not available Notify Immediately report suspected and confirmed cases of novel influenza to Public Health at 206-296-4774, including patients with ARI and identified epidemiologic risk factors. Do not wait for lab confirmation before notifying us. The following are immediately notifiable: All suspected novel influenza, including avian influenza (influenza A H5 or others); a negative influenza PCR does not rule out avian influenza All influenza A specimens that result as "unsubtypeable" CONTACT Communicable Diseases Epidemiology and Immunization Section 401 5th Ave, Suite 1250 Seattle, WA 98104 Phone: 206-296-4774 TTY Relay: 711 Fax: 206-296-4803 Provider Alert: Testing and Subtyping for Avian Influenza, WA State Dept. of Health Influenza Virus Testing at the Washington State Public Health Laboratories (PHL) including Novel Influenza and Fatal Influenza Influenza Specimen Collection and submission Instructions, WA State Dept. of Health Influenza Specimen Collection, CDC A(H5) Bird Flu: Current Situation | Bird Flu, CDC Three years ago, in UK Novel Flu Surveillance: Quantifying TTD, we looked at a UKHSA report that it would likely take between 3 and 10 weeks before community spread of a novel flu virus would become apparent to authorities, after anywhere between a few dozen to a few thousand community infections In 2024 the ECDC issued guidance for member nations on Enhanced Influenza Surveillance to Detect Avian Influenza Virus Infections in the EU/EEA During the Inter-Seasonal Period., which cautioned: Sentinel surveillance systems are important for the monitoring of respiratory viruses in the EU/EEA, but these systems are not designed and are not sufficiently sensitive to identify a newly emerging virus such as avian influenza in the general population early enough for the purpose of implementing control measures in a timely way. A sobering reminder that, while we comfort ourselves with our current low number of human novel flu detections, we are probably missing some cases. Tuesday, October 20, 2026 Washington State Confirms 5 More Dairy Herds Infected With H5N1 (n=8) Credit Washington State Dept Ag. #19,380 Not quite 2 weeks ago the USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State, which was followed a week later by the first (reportedly mild) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection). Details, such as the genotype, how cattle may have been infected, and the exact exposure (apparently, dairy cattle related) of the human case have yet to be released. On Oct 8th, the USDA stated "APHIS will complete genetic sequencing and announce final results as soon as they are available.", but thus far I've seen nothing published. Screenshot taken today, Oct 20th, 2026. Three days ago I posted Washington State Confirms 3rd Dairy Herd Infected With H5N1, which was apparently reported on the 15th. Yesterday the USDA and Washington State Department of Agriculture added 5 more herds, all reportedly in Yakima County. Other than the above updated dashboards and graphics, I've found no other information on these latest developments. As mentioned previously, Washington is one of the few U.S. states that allows the sale of raw milk in grocery stores, natural food markets, food co-ops, and direct-to-consumer farm stores. While I'm confident that pasteurization effectively kills the H5N1 virus in commercial milk, raw milk (and milk products) are a different matter. In 2024 and 2025 we saw a number of high profile reports of pets infected with H5N1 via raw milk and/or raw pet food (see Washington State (WSDA) Announces 2 Households with H5N1 Infected Cats Linked to Raw Food). On Oct 8th, the State of Washington issued this warning: Dairy product safety Pasteurization inactivates viruses and bacteria in milk, including HPAI virus, helping ensure the safety of the dairy supply. Roy Graber October 22, 2026 Flogel | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) has killed more than 77,000 birds across three commercial poultry flocks in Alberta, Canada, with the largest outbreak affecting a flock of 69,001 broilers in Strathcona County. Total birds lost: More than 77,000 birds across three commercial flocks in Alberta Largest outbreak: 69,001 commercial broilers in Strathcona County confirmed October 8 Virus type: All cases confirmed as H5N1 subtype of highly pathogenic avian influenza Other affected flocks: 2,444 ducks in Sturgeon County (October 7) and 5,632 mixed birds in Two Hills County (October 1) Additional cases: CFIA confirmed HPAI in three more flocks, though two were later identified as noncommercial operations When highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) struck three commercial poultry flocks in Alberta, Canada, this fall, more than 77,000 birds were lost, according to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). The largest of the three flocks was in Strathcona County, a case the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) previously announced was confirmed Oct. 8. A WOAH report revealed that the flock contained 69,001 commercial broilers. Another infection, which CFIA reported was confirmed Oct. 7, involved 2,444 ducks at a commercial duck breeder farm in Sturgeon County. The third flock listed in the WOAH report was a commercial mixed flock of 5,632 broilers, turkeys and geese in Two Hills County. HPAI was confirmed there Oct. 1. In all three cases, the virus detected was the H5N1 subtype. CFIA has also confirmed HPAI in three more poultry flocks in the province, one each in Sturgeon, Foothills and Northern Lights counties. However, the flocks in Northern Lights and Foothills counties have since been identified as noncommercial. Manitoba flock reclassified In a separate report, WOAH revealed that an HPAI case in Gimli, Manitoba, which CFIA had previously reported as a commercial poultry flock, involved a backyard nonpoultry flock of 17 birds. CFIA has since changed its online report to show that the flock was not being raised for commercial purposes. To learn more about HPAI cases in commercial poultry flocks in the United States, Mexico and Canada, see an interactive map on WATTPoultry.com. Roy Graber October 22, 2026 Flogel | Bigstock Article Summary Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) has killed more than 77,000 birds across three commercial poultry flocks in Alberta, Canada, with the largest outbreak affecting a flock of 69,001 broilers in Strathcona County. Total birds lost: More than 77,000 birds across three commercial flocks in Alberta Largest outbreak: 69,001 commercial broilers in Strathcona County confirmed October 8 Virus type: All cases confirmed as H5N1 subtype of highly pathogenic avian influenza Other affected flocks: 2,444 ducks in Sturgeon County (October 7) and 5,632 mixed birds in Two Hills County (October 1) Additional cases: CFIA confirmed HPAI in three more flocks, though two were later identified as noncommercial operations When highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) struck three commercial poultry flocks in Alberta, Canada, this fall, more than 77,000 birds were lost, according to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). The largest of the three flocks was in Strathcona County, a case the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) previously announced was confirmed Oct. 8. A WOAH report revealed that the flock contained 69,001 commercial broilers. Another infection, which CFIA reported was confirmed Oct. 7, involved 2,444 ducks at a commercial duck breeder farm in Sturgeon County. The third flock listed in the WOAH report was a commercial mixed flock of 5,632 broilers, turkeys and geese in Two Hills County. HPAI was confirmed there Oct. 1. In all three cases, the virus detected was the H5N1 subtype. CFIA has also confirmed HPAI in three more poultry flocks in the province, one each in Sturgeon, Foothills and Northern Lights counties. However, the flocks in Northern Lights and Foothills counties have since been identified as noncommercial. Manitoba flock reclassified In a separate report, WOAH revealed that an HPAI case in Gimli, Manitoba, which CFIA had previously reported as a commercial poultry flock, involved a backyard nonpoultry flock of 17 birds. CFIA has since changed its online report to show that the flock was not being raised for commercial purposes. To learn more about HPAI cases in commercial poultry flocks in the United States, Mexico and Canada, see an interactive map on WATTPoultry.com. records.content_title: Avian Flu Confirmed in Commercial Poultry Flock in Barron County
records.content: MADISON, WI — The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) has identified a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County. DATCP and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) animal health officials are working together in a joint incident response. The affected premises has been quarantined to restrict movement of poultry and poultry products. Birds on the property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. Birds from the flock will not enter the food system. The HPAI virus has continued to circulate in both wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021. HPAI viruses are highly contagious and often fatal to domestic poultry. Caused by influenza type A viruses, the disease varies in severity depending on the strain and species affected. The disease can be spread by contact with infected birds, commingling with wild birds or their droppings, equipment, or clothing worn by anyone working with the animals. DATCP continues to urge all livestock owners to implement strong biosecurity measures to protect their flocks and herds from the disease. This includes washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals, and separating new additions to the flock or herd for at least 30 days. Poultry owners are asked, when possible, to keep their birds indoors. When HPAI is diagnosed in a Wisconsin poultry flock, a control area is established within a 10-kilometer area around the infected premises, restricting movement on or off any premises with poultry. To help producers determine if their poultry are located within an active control area or surveillance zone, poultry owners are encouraged to use DATCP's mapping tool . DATCP reminds Wisconsin livestock owners to register their premises. State law requires that all livestock owners register where their animals are kept. Poultry is included in the definition of livestock for premises registration. Registration helps animal health officials communicate with flock and herd owners during disease outbreaks. To report increased mortality or signs of illness among domestic birds, dairy cattle, or other animals, contact DATCP by following the instructions on the Animal Disease Reporting webpage . For updates on how the virus is affecting domestic birds in Wisconsin, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin poultry, visit DATCP’s HPAI in Poultry webpage . HPAI in Other Species The HPAI virus has continued to circulate in both wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021. Since that time, the HPAI virus has also affected other species, including mammalian species. DATCP continues to work with USDA to conduct testing for HPAI, encourage biosecurity, and provide resources to producers. For updates on how the HPAI virus is affecting dairy cattle across the country, and to find resources on protecting Wisconsin dairy cattle, visit DATCP’s HPAI in Dairy Cattle webpage . records.content_title: Louisville Zoo closes some habitats after wild goose tests positive for avian flu
records.content: LOUISVILLE, Ky. — The Louisville Zoo has temporarily shut down certain bird areas after an ill wild Canada goose found on zoo grounds tested positive for avian influenza, according to a news release. Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, or bird flu, is a viral illness that mainly affects wild and domestic birds, the release said. This naturally occurs in wild bird groups and has the potential to spread to other birds and, occasionally, to other animals. Zoo Director Dan Maloney said the disease has been in the area for a few years. “Our animal care, veterinary and operations teams are trained and prepared to respond to emerging health concerns for the protection of our animals,” Maloney said. He said that temporary closures help the zoo minimize risks to the animals and guarantee a safe experience for visitors. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the risk to the public is very low. The zoo said that none of its birds are showing signs of the disease, and that the zoo will remain open while limiting access to bird habitats. “We continuously monitor avian influenza activity in our region and have established measures to reduce potential exposure to zoo animals,” said Dr. Zoli Gyimesi, zoo senior veterinarian. The zoo plans to observe both its birds and any wild birds around the grounds for avian influenza, following developments and updating protocols accordingly. According to the zoo, guests can help by not feeding wild birds or other wildlife while visiting the zoo. Feeding geese and ducks causes them to gather in spaces frequented by guests and zoo animals, the zoo said

records.content_title: Avian flu was primary cause of death for Big Bear bald eagle Jackie, necropsy findings show
records.content: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) was the primary underlying cause of death for Jackie, a bald eagle known to viewers of a livestream from Big Bear Valley in California, according to necropsy and diagnostic findings released October 14 by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).1 For more than a decade, viewers around the world followed Jackie and her mate, Shadow, as they nested and raised eaglets. Jackie, who was about 14 years old, died in August after weeks of treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center in California. She had been treated for several health problems, including anemia. After her death, veterinary pathologists at San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance performed a necropsy, followed by additional laboratory and toxicology testing, according to CDFW.1 “Jackie's necropsy confirmed...HPAI as the primary underlying cause of her decline,” Steven Kubiski, DVM, PhD, DACVP, director of disease investigations at the alliance, said in a statement released by CDFW. The infection caused an unusual complication: a severe stomach ulcer that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and bacterial sepsis, he said.1 A stomach ulcer led to further complications Pathologists found chronic disease in Jackie's ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach commonly known as the gizzard. The ulcerated tissue caused ongoing blood loss and severe anemia and provided a pathway for bacteria to enter her body, resulting in a secondary infection, according to CDFW. Testing also revealed severe inflammation and blood clots in her heart and several major blood vessels. HPAI genetic material was detected in multiple tissues, including the ulcerated ventriculus.1 Additional testing ruled out West Nile virus. Heavy metal levels, including lead, were within acceptable limits and were not considered a factor in the progression of her illness, CDFW said. Toxicology screening detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in Jackie's liver, along with persistent environmental contaminants. However, the necropsy did not reveal the uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with anticoagulant rodenticide exposure. CDFW therefore did not identify brodifacoum as the primary cause of her illness or death. The US Department of Agriculture National Veterinary Services Laboratories provided final confirmation of the HPAI infection, according to the agency. CDFW said the findings indicated that several severe, interconnected disease processes developed over time and ultimately led to Jackie's death. The diagnosis was unexpected During Jackie's hospitalization, clinicians at the Ojai Raptor Center investigated several possible causes of her illness, including lead poisoning, zinc toxicity, rodenticide poisoning, and cancer. She also received a blood transfusion, USA Today reported.2 The HPAI diagnosis came as a surprise because Jackie did not exhibit the clinical signs typically associated with the infection in eagles, and no active outbreak had been reported in the area, William Bowerman, a professor of wildlife ecology and environmental toxicology at the University of Maryland, told USA Today.2 Chris Eksteen, MEd, executive director of the Ojai Raptor Center, said the necropsy findings helped explain observations the team made during Jackie's treatment, according to the CDFW release.1 HPAI continues to circulate among wild birds HPAI continues to circulate in wild bird populations across the United States, according to CDFW. Waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts of avian influenza viruses, whereas eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating infected prey, the agency said.1 Bald eagles feed largely on fish and waterfowl. Waterfowl can carry avian influenza viruses without showing signs of illness, increasing the risk that predators will consume infected birds, according to the National Park Service. Eagles may also eat sick birds or recently dead carcasses, providing another route of exposure.3 The US Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository cremated Jackie's remains under established procedures intended to prevent the spread of HPAI to wildlife and humans. CDFW said camera footage provided no evidence that Shadow or the pair's eaglets were ill.1 “Jackie’s death also marked the loss of one half of the iconic bald eagle pair that has occupied Big Bear Valley for years. Her mate, Shadow, remains in Big Bear. Based on camera data, we have no evidence that Shadow or the eaglets were sick,” CDFW wrote in its announcement.1 The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015. Bald eagle populations in the United States rebounded after the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were implemented, allowing the species to be removed from the federal endangered species list.4 References Necropsy provides new information about beloved bald eagle known as Jackie. (WDRB+WAVE) — The Louisville Zoo is closing parts of its bird areas after a positive avian influenza test. In a statement, the zoo said a wild Canada goose tested positive for avian flu after staff found it sick on zoo grounds. As a precaution, public walk-through aviaries will be temporarily closed while the Zoo awaits the results of confirmatory testing at a federal lab. The closures include the Forest Bird Trail and African penguin exhibits in the Islands Pavilion, Stellar’s Sea Eagle Aviary in Glacier Run, Lorikeet Landing in Australia and some areas near the zoo’s lake. Officials said the sections will remain closed for several weeks as they wait for the threat of spread to subside. Additional biosecurity measures have also been implemented for zookeepers who work directly with birds. “HPAI has been known in our region for the past few years and our animal care, veterinary and operations teams are trained and prepared to respond to emerging health concerns for the protection of our animals,” Louisville Zoo Director Dan Maloney said. “We are implementing these additional precautionary measures to further reduce risk to the animals in our care. 佛山大学兽医学科底蕴深厚,在禽流感防控研究中曾取得过开创性成果。人口密度大、跨境流动频繁、气候高温高湿、人畜共患病风险复杂等区域新特征,让这所高校的兽医学科发展急需一位既熟悉国家重大疫病“攻坚战”打法,又能打通产学研全链条的领军人才。 2023年,张克山出任佛山大学兽医学科带头人。这位深耕动物疫病防控二十余年的研究员,从中国农业科学院兰州兽医研究所南下,任佛山大学科学研究部(校地合作办公室)部长、校学术委员会副主任、动物科技学院三级教授、博士生导师。他以学科带头人和科研管理者的双重身份,推动佛山大学兽医学科开启高质量“二次创业”:由华南传统兽医研究阵地,向服务粤港澳大湾区生物安全的战略支点转型。 引才补链:学科方向实现“南北嫁接” 张克山此前在中国农业科学院兰州兽医研究所工作十余年,曾任国家口蹄疫参考实验室核心骨干,主要从事口蹄疫、非洲猪瘟等重大动物烈性传染病与人畜共患传染病的基础研究和防控产品研发。他参与研发的口蹄疫O型、A型二价灭活疫苗获国家一类新兽药证书并实现产业化,累计销售疫苗收入超过23亿元。这段科研履历,恰好可以帮助佛山大学兽医学科在重大动物烈性传染病、人畜共患病领域国家级科研等方面发力。 “北方打的是口蹄疫、非洲猪瘟这类重大疫病的攻坚战;大湾区要面对的是人口密度大、虫媒病毒活跃、跨境病原输入、多病原混感的系统战。”张克山将西北积累的科研经验与华南区域特点有机融合,带领学科确立了人畜共患病溯源、新发疫病解析、动物生物安全三大方向,将防控关口从“人间发病”前移至“动物带毒”阶段,落实国家“关口前移”防控方针。 筑强阵地:科研攻关取得标志性突破 方向的重构,很快在科研端兑现。 2025年,佛山大学兽医学科相关团队在H5N1禽流感病毒受体结合特异性演变研究方向取得重大突破,成果以研究快报(Letter)形式发表于国际顶级期刊《Science》。佛山大学为论文第一单位,青年教师温峰教授为第一作者,在教授黄淑坚、张克山共同指导下,联合华南农业大学、江西农业大学、中国农业科学院上海兽医研究所科研团队共同完成。 该研究系统解析了H5N1病毒血凝素(HA)受体结合特异性的演变规律,首次发现N193K突变可显著增强病毒对人源唾液酸(α2,6)受体的亲和力;结合既往报道与本团队数据,进一步明确了N193D、Q226L等位点在病毒适应人源受体过程中的作用。这是佛山大学首次以第一通讯单位在《Science》刊发研究成果,也是继2024年12月在《Lancet Microbe》发表论文之后取得的又一项重大突破。 “学科发展不能只盯着论文和项目,要着力破解大湾区发展中的现实难题。”在张克山推动下,佛山大学兽医学科搭起“基础研究—技术开发—产业应用”全链条,研发适配中小养殖主体的低成本生物安全方案,通过“一博士对接一企业”的校地合作机制,将技术红利输送至湾区畜牧养殖、动物保健、动物性食品等产业链一线。 服务地方:推动科研成果落地转化 作为学科带头人兼学校科学研究部部长,张克山的角色不止于“带团队做科研”。他将二十余年科研积累,转化为学科建设与学校创新发展的双重动能:一方面推动兽医学科与海关口岸、疾控中心、粤港澳相关机构建立联合联防机制,助力大湾区跨境生物安全联防联控;另一方面搭建分层分类人才培养体系,并着重培育科研攻坚、学科交叉、服务地方三类人才,持续为湾区输送高素质兽医力量。 在科研管理上,他主导广东省市场监督管理局“2025年广东数据知识产权推广服务”项目,推动学校完成24件高质量科研数据采集确权并取得证书,打造“佛大特色数据池”。2025年,他代表佛山大学与佛山医药集团签署全面战略合作协议,推动科研成果转化、产业链协同和人才培育;同年6月,代表佛山大学与黔东南州科技局签署科技合作协议。他还带队赴东莞市动物疫病预防控制中心开展交流访问,推进校地协同育人与有组织科研。 张克山主持国家重点研发计划课题、国家自然科学基金等国家级及省部级项目10余项,以第一或通讯作者发表英文论文60余篇、中文核心论文80余篇,申请专利157项,其中98项已获授权,主编、副主编著作10多部,斩获神农中华农业科技奖科学研究类成果一等奖、甘肃省科技进步奖二等奖、中国专利优秀奖等多项重要科技奖励。 从西北戈壁到岭南水乡,变的是场景,不变的是服务国家生物安全的底色。张克山表示,未来团队将继续围绕国家动物生物安全重大需求,病原与宿主互作机制研究,完善“基础研究—技术开发—产业应用”全链条创新体系,聚焦动物疫苗、诊断试剂和药物研发,推动更多成果在粤港澳大湾区落地转化,为筑牢我国动物疫病防控科技防线、助力农业强国建设贡献更多力量。 编辑:麦锦婷 责任编辑:徐静 佛山大学 科研 点击收起全文
